Six other children were present, but none were physically harmed, authorities said.

Authorities have not released any information about a potential motive for the killings. They said there was no history of police calls to the Hopkins address.

Records show that Kristen Brown had been licensed by the state since 2019. The daycare had a capacity of 10 children and was found to be in compliance during visits in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Family members of Kristen Brown declined to comment on Thursday.

Kristen Brown opened Brown Bear Childcare a few months after giving birth to Evie. In a 2019 post on the daycare's Facebook page, Brown wrote that she hoped to help her daughter and other children "blossom into happy, intelligent, caring individuals."

Kristen Brown had a bachelor's degree in elementary education foundations from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities and was certified in vision therapy, according to her daycare's Facebook page. She incorporated music and cooking classes into her days with the children and would take them on field trips to a science museum and an orchard.

title: I was too pregnant to pitch my business on 'Shark Tank.' My husband and Pete Davidson went instead.
description: Allison Strumeyer says ordering 10,000 pairs of socks before launching doublesoul helped prove demand and gave her the confidence to build the company.
fullText:
Allison Strumeyer wanted experience in finance and a startup before launching her own.

She says working for BlackRock showed her how to work to a high standard.

She launched a sock company that does millions in annual sales.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Allison Strumeyer, cofounder and CEO of doublesoul. It has been edited for length and clarity.

When I was in college at the University of Pennsylvania, I had a side hustle selling T-shirts. I would connect with local artists to feature their work and sell the shirts on campus. I also did pitch competitions with my now-husband, Ben. I've always felt very native to entrepreneurship, and I knew I wanted to start my own business.

Yet, when I graduated, I chose to work at BlackRock. It was intentional: I believed working with a global finance company would give me insights valuable to me as an entrepreneur. BlackRock also taught me how to perform at a high level, in everything from communications to project management.

I was at BlackRock for about two years, then joined Mirror, a startup that was acquired by Lululemon. Mirror was smaller and scrappier, and during my four years there, I learned about scaling a startup. The combination of both experiences left me ready to start my own company.

I always found it interesting that we wear socks more than almost anything else in our wardrobe. But there's little innovation, product development, branding, or design around socks. I felt the category had been ignored, and I believed that we all deserve socks we're excited about.

My husband Ben and I became really emotionally attached to the idea of creating better socks. But we wanted to test the market before diving in. We created a prototype and ordered 10,000 pairs — the minimum order, which was about $100,000 worth of socks.

We shared them with pretty much everyone we'd ever met and asked them to post about the socks. That gave us organic sales and — more importantly — proof of our concept. In 2022, we officially launched Doublesoul.

I chose to stay in my day job as long as possible while we started the company. On social media, people are encouraged to leave their jobs to pursue their own projects, but that felt like dangerous territory to me.

Having that backing gave me the confidence I needed to leave my job. Ben and I knew we would need to sell lots of socks before we could fund a team. But we also wanted to move quickly, so we pursued venture funding. We raised about $2 million.

title: I Tried the Android App That's Helping People Around the World Bypass Censorship Laws
description: You can now run Snowflake Volunteer on any Android phone.
fullText:
If you've read our previous coverage on the Tor network and the Tor Browser, you'll know they're the best choices if you want to maximize your privacy and anonymity on the internet. Now, the Tor project has teamed up with the Bloco Android app studio to release another app focused on privacy and anonymity: Snowflake Volunteer.

This isn't only bout keeping your own browsing safe and secure—if you install it on your Android phone, you're helping other people circumvent censorship restrictions in their current location, donating part of your connection to the web so that they can get online at all.

The Tor Browser is so effective at hiding the identity and online activities of users that certain governments would rather their citizens didn't make use of it. That takes away one of the best privacy browsers in the business for the people of those countries, and anyone who happens to be visiting them. Censoring the Tor Browser is usually done by refusing access to the relay nodes that it routes traffic around—the stops on the way to and from the internet that do the job of concealing locations and other identifiable information. However, the relay directory is public, which means it can be blocked.

That's where Snowflake comes in. The standalone Android app is new, but the idea isn't. Snowflake is an alternative way the Tor Browser can get online: A Snowflake connection is disguised as a standard video call over the WebRTC protocol, which isn't typically restricted, and from there, a connection can be made to the Tor network.

With Snowflake on your phone, you're essentially smuggling someone in a Tor-restricted country across the border, digitally speaking. Even if these intermediate bridges are detected and blocked, they're short-lived, with new ones continually popping up, making it virtually impossible for a government to block this method of access without crippling much of the general internet in their country.

The Tor Browser runs as normal for the user who's connecting, albeit with the standard trade-offs in terms of speed and latency. Because of the rerouting and technical borrowing that goes on, Tor isn't the best option if you want to maximize your broadband upload and download speeds.

As a firm believer that internet users should be able to get on the web with a high level of anonymity and privacy, I installed the new Snowflake Volunteer app from the Google Play Store (it's also on F-Droid) and powered it up. The first job is to exempt it from battery management rules so it will stay available even if it's not being used, a process the app guides you through.

That done, all that's required is enabling the toggle switch on the main screen, and your phone is ready and waiting for someone else to connect. There's no setup configuration to work through, no user account to create, and everything works automatically in the background—it really is designed to be as simple as possible.

Tap on the settings cog (top right), and you'll find a few settings at your disposal: You can opt to only allow connections when you're on unmetered networks (such as wifi) or when your phone is charging. You can also set how many users your phone can support at any one time. This is all in the interest of limiting the impact on your device.

Across four hours or so, I saw six connections made, sending a total of 3.2 megabytes and receiving a total of 17 megabytes—hardly excessive use. My phone wasn't suddenly overrun with other users wanting to get online. Snowflake Volunteer is designed as an emergency measure for circumventing censorship, and the usage I've seen backs that up.

I didn't notice any bugs or any problems with the app or any impact on my battery life (perhaps to be expected with so little activity). I think it's something I'll keep switched on, especially overnight when I'm not using my device. It's a nice idea to be able to see the stats on how many people you've helped over time, as an encouragement to keep your device available.

As a Snowflake Volunteer, you're not at risk of being identified by any state that's censored the Tor project: To them, you look like a standard audio or video call connection, and there's no static list of IP addresses to block. What's more, the same multiple layers of encryption that protect the entire Tor network are still in place, so you're unable to see anything connecting users are doing, and they will go through several more nodes before doing any browsing anyway—your device is just the entry point. No one who connects to your device can learn anything about you: The app is simply not capable of any sort of surveillance. You're loaning a slice of connectivity, anonymously and securely. (There are more details of how it all works in Tor's Snowflake documentation.)

The new Android app isn't your only option for putting your hand up as a Snowflake volunteer. You can also install the desktop browser add-on or enable the Kindness Mode in the Orbot app for iOS (a VPN that enables connections to the Tor network).

title: Here's How Google's New 'Tap to Share' Android Feature Works
description: You'll be able to share files and contact info by bringing your Android phones together.
fullText:
Google made a lot of announcements on Wednesday, all of them hours before its official Made by Google event. The company announced the new Pixel 11 series (including the Pixel 11 Pro Fold), the Galaxy Watch 5, and even the long-rumored Pixel Tag. There were so many announcements, one would be forgiven for assuming it was a hardware-only event.

And yet, Google also revealed a number of software features, as well. The Pixel Watch received much of the attention here, as the company announced that its smartwatches will soon track trends in insulin resistance, blood pressure, and sleep habits, but the Pixel wasn't left out of the conversation either. In fact, Android devices across the board are getting one new feature that seems particularly useful: Tap to Share.

Tap to Share appears to live up to its name. According to Google, all you need to do to use it is take your compatible Android device and place it near another compatible Android device. When you do, you'll pull up each other's contact cards, making it an easy way to share phone numbers, email addresses, and other contact info with someone new on Android.

However, the feature isn't limited to digital business cards. You can also use it to share photos, videos, and other files from your Android to another. To use it, open the file in question, then launch the Share Sheet. Then, bring your phone close to the other user's. Now, instead of your contact cards, Android will send over your file.

While Google might have announced this feature alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, it works with a lot of Google phones. The company says you'll be able to use Tap to Share on Pixel 6 and newer, which spans the entirety of Google's current supported Pixel devices. In addition, Google says Tap to Share is coming to some Samsung Galaxy phones, including the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Fold 8, and Flip 8, and will expand to even more devices by the end of 2026.

Tap to Share is, of course, similar to Apple's NameDrop feature on iOS, down to the contact card default. However, Android beat Apple to the punch originally. This is essentially an evolution of Android Beam, a discontinued feature that let you send data over NFC. And while the feature won't work with iPhones, Google and Apple do offer a quick sharing option for users trying to share from Android to iPhone, and vice versa.

title: Taiwan says it was targeted last month in AI-driven hacking campaign
description: Taiwan detected AI-assisted cyberattacks on government agencies last month coming from overseas but the affected bodies
fullText:
TAIPEI/WASHINGTON, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Taiwan detected AI-assisted cyberattacks on government agencies last month coming from overseas but the affected bodies successfully "handled" the incident, the Ministry of Digital Affairs said on Thursday.

Taiwan has in ‌recent years complained about what it sees as China's "hybrid warfare" — from daily military drills near the island to disinformation campaigns and ‌cyberattacks — as Beijing ramps up military and political pressure on the democratically governed island to force Taipei to accept its claims of sovereignty.

Chinese cyberattacks on Taiwan's key infrastructure ​from hospitals to banks rose 6% in 2025 from the previous year to an average of 2.63 million attacks a day, the island's National Security Bureau said in January, adding some of the hacks were synchronised with military drills in "hybrid threats" to paralyse the island.

In a statement, the Ministry of Digital Affairs said its cybersecurity monitoring units detected the "abnormal attack" targeting government agencies in July, and beginning July 20, its National Institute ‌of Cyber Security issued a series of warning ⁠alerts while it investigated.

The investigation results showed the attacks displayed clear characteristics of an "overseas source", with hackers employing a hybrid approach that combined manual operations with AI agent-assisted attacks, such as Open Claw, it said.

"The relevant ⁠attack sources, methods, and scope of impact have all been fully investigated, and the affected units have successively completed their handling," the ministry added.

In response to this new type of AI-derived cybersecurity threat, the government has established protective guidelines and strengthened system monitoring across agencies to block attacks early, it ​said.

The statement ​did not mention China, and China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately ​respond to a request for comment on the attack.

Taiwan's statement came a day after the Israeli cybersecurity company Dream said in a blog post that it had uncovered an AI-driven hacking campaign that stole credentials and other data from an unnamed government in Asia.

Dream said a team of AI agents worked together to extract scores of passwords from unidentified officials, steal personnel records from Taiwan's justice ministry, and scan its nuclear safety agency for vulnerabilities over the course of four days.

Dream, which said it was able to reconstruct the hacking campaign after recovering the agents' "complete operational workspace," declined to share ‌the data or name the government when approached by Reuters, but the Financial ​Times, which was the first media outlet briefed on Dream's findings, identified the target ​agencies as Taiwanese.

The threat of AI-assisted hacking campaigns ​has been growing for years but ramped up dramatically over the past few months after top AI labs ‌released models, such as Anthropic's Mythos, which can rapidly conduct ​reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities, and take advantage ​of them.

Cris Thomas, a researcher who works as a security advocate at the code security company Semgrep, said the spy campaign was an illustration of just how quickly AI-assisted hackers could hit their mark.

Thomas cautioned against exaggerating the power of AI agents, ​however.

"There's still a human in there somewhere. Somebody ‌had to choose who to attack, had to establish an objective and give it a directive. It's not totally ​100% autonomous. There was a capable operator in charge that did that," he added.

title: Hodgkinson into 800m final and Werro through despite nasty fall
description: Keely Hodgkinson reaches the women's 800m final at the European Championships - moments after rival Audrey Werro suffers a dramatic fall that put her place in doubt.
fullText:
Keely Hodgkinson's bid for European gold continued as she stormed into the final of the women's 800m - moments after rival Audrey Werro suffered a dramatic fall that put her place in Friday's showpiece in doubt.

Werro - who ran the fastest time for 43 years earlier this season - led from the start in the first semi-final, but crashed to the floor on the final bend in Birmingham.

The Swiss 22-year-old got back to her feet a moment later and finished the race in last place, grimacing and clutching her chest.

However, Werro will race against Hodgkinson in a highly anticipated final following a successful appeal, with footage showing France's Anais Bourgoin had hit Werro's right foot with her left hand.

An earlier angle had appeared to show Werro clipping her own leg before falling.

There was less drama in the second semi-final, with Hodgkinson safely crossing the line first in one minute 57.38 seconds.

The Olympic champion led from the start and held off the fast-improving Femke Broeders-Bol - a two-time world 400m hurdles champion who chose to switch events this season - to advance.

Asked if she had seen Werro's fall before her race, Hodgkinson told BBC TV: "I heard an 'ooh' [from the crowd] which is never a good sign. I don't know what it looked like."

Speaking before Werro's appeal, Hodgkinson added: "Obviously it's a real shame and I hope she's OK.

"I hope she's in the final tomorrow [Friday], that'd be a really exciting race."

The women's 800m has become the must-watch event of the championships because of the expected three-way battle between Hodgkinson, Werro and Broeders-Bol.

"The excitement makes me excited. I can't wait to step out there. It brings out the best in me," Hodgkinson added.

"I love a good challenge. Hopefully it'll be a good race, a clean race, nobody falling over."

Hodgkinson will be joined in the final by fellow Briton Jemma Reekie, who capitalised on Werro's fall to win the first semi-final.

There will be 10 athletes in Friday's final instead of nine, with Lithuanian athlete Gabija Galvydyte - who was clipped by Werro as she fell - also advancing.

The opening semi-final was panning out as expected until Werro suddenly stumbled and fell face first onto the track with just under 140m left to go.

"It was a hard hit on the floor. These tracks are incredibly hard, especially when they've been sun-baked," former Olympic long jump champion Greg Rutherford said on BBC TV.

"It really was a difficult thing to watch, and you're just hoping at that point [that] there's no serious injury."

Werro appeared to be in some discomfort, rolling onto her side and clutching her chest before getting back up and finishing the race at a slow jog.

Paula Radcliffe, a former women's marathon world record holder, said: "Athletes know if that happens and you go down, you have to get up and finish.

"That is the only criteria that you're going to make it through. If you don't do that, you have no chance of being advanced through to that final.

"You could see she was not comfortable."

However, there was considerable confusion over whether Werro had tripped herself or been impeded by another athlete.

Rutherford believed Werro had "kicked her own leg", while former men's 1500m world champion Steve Cram said she had "tripped herself".

Werro herself did not know, telling BBC TV: "I was feeling great but unfortunately I don't know, something happened and then I was on the ground."

A closer look at the footage showed that Bourgoin, who had been on Werro's shoulder for much of the race, disrupted the Swiss athlete's rhythm with a slight touch to her foot with her left hand.

"The question is whether Werro is OK - it was a really hard fall," Cram said.

"But we are getting the final we wanted. That's one way to look at it."

A successful appeal by Werro means fans will be treated to a blockbuster final featuring three of the biggest names in world athletics right now - including home hope Hodgkinson.

The 24-year-old has won the past two European titles and will be hoping to defend her crown following a successful season that has seen her break the long-standing indoor 800m world record, win her first world title and improve her British record outdoors.

An added incentive for Hodgkinson will be the chance to break the longest-standing world record in athletics.

No-one has broken Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova's 800m time of 1:53.28 seconds that was set back in 1983. There have been claims that Kratochvilova's performance in Munich was assisted by the systematic doping regime that existed in her country at the time - something she has strenuously denied.

It is Werro, however, who has come closest to breaking that record.

She has run three of the nine fastest women's 800m times in history during a superb unbeaten outdoor season.

After improving to 1:53.80 seconds in June - the third fastest in history - Werro's personal best is more than half a second faster than Hodgkinson's 1:54.33.

But there will be a new contender for Hodgkinson and Werro to be wary of in the form of Broeders-Bol.

Still largely an unknown in the 800m after deciding to switch disciplines from 400m hurdles, the Dutch athlete impressed at the Paris Diamond League event in June with a time of 1:55.60.

"Femke looked as though she had another gear there but didn't use it - she didn't need to expend any more energy," Radcliffe said after Broeders-Bol finished close behind Hodgkinson in the semi-finals.

"We know Keely has the endurance, but does Femke have that endurance to bounce back for three rounds? "

title: Shuttered Colleges Are Selling The Only Asset They Have Left: Their Campuses
description: Vast swaths of land and buildings are on the market, with more to come as financially distressed schools close around the country.
fullText:
(Bloomberg) -- Trinity Christian College moved fast. Even before its final graduating class walked the stage in May, the private school put its 60-acre Illinois campus on the market.

Walter Sells Lakers, Seeks More Cash to Pay Loans Amid DOJ Probe

Phoebe Gates Knew Phia Shopping App Took Credit for Sales It Didn't Drive

Trump Seeks Immediate Halt to Judge's Penalties in IRS Case

Anthropic Said in Talks to Buy Startup Decart for $6 Billion

Trump Weighs Call for Capital Gains Tax Cuts as Midterm Boost

It needed a buyer that not only would take on the land, but also the 22 school buildings, including dorms, science labs and a 1,200-seat chapel with a pipe organ, that came with it. Late last month, one came through: Chicago Christian Schools acquired the college in a deal that fully pays off municipal bondholders who financed Trinity before its financial collapse.

It's a rare, optimal outcome in a brutal era for higher education. Driven by shifting demographics and mounting debt, over 50 US colleges have closed or merged since 2020. That distress has put thousands of acres of classrooms, dorms and athletic facilities on the real estate market, many in need of redevelopment.

For shuttered schools, selling campuses has become critical to repaying bondholders who increasingly view the real estate as a backstop for their investments. For communities built around those institutions, the sales can reshape entire towns as developers convert campuses into housing, medical centers, luxury resorts or other uses — or, if no buyer emerges, they're left with vacant reminders of a vanished academic institution. About a dozen schools currently have campuses in limbo, according to a Bloomberg analysis.

"In so many of these smaller towns, the college is the economic engine," said David Carlos, a broker with JLL who has worked on real estate deals with more than two dozen colleges, including St. John's University, College of Saint Rose and Hebrew Union College. "So losing those jobs, losing that economic development, is a real blow."

Trinity Christian's May closure hit Palos Heights' grocery stores, pizza parlors and coffee shops, said Mayor Robert Straz. The local businesses had been accustomed to the college students, faculty and families frequenting their establishments for six decades.

The fate of campuses stands to become an even more pressing issue in coming years as enrollment declines and rising expenses lead to deeper strains for schools. More than 400 private colleges in the US will close or merge over the coming decade, according to Huron, a consulting firm that advises higher education institutions. That's more than a quarter of all of the country's existing private colleges.

"Minnesotans are exhausted, and John, quite frankly, they're embarrassed. I have talked to hundreds of voters in Minnesota who have told me, 'Gosh, I went on vacation this summer. I didn't want to tell people where I was from because it's embarrassing.' And it's true," she said, detailing how Democrats in the North Star State are wary of shifts in the party toward socialism.

Democrats are set to begin the Minnesota Senate general election with an advantage, according to the early polling from Mason-Dixon Polling & Research. It did not poll specific candidates but reported that Democrats lead Republicans on the generic ballot in the Senate race, 49 percent to 41 percent.

Flanagan is backed by Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.), who chose not to seek reelection, and has also received support from progressive leaders, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).

She has been outspoken on the campaign trail for universal healthcare and ending U.S. military aid for Israel.

Flanagan served as lieutenant governor during the state's widespread money laundering scheme, which is estimated to have stolen as much as roughly $9 billion and could present problems for Flanagan come November.

National Republican Senatorial Committee chair Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) issued a statement in support of Tafoya, saying "Peggy Flanagan oversaw the worst fraud scandal in modern American history and is now running as one of the most radical socialist Senate candidates on the map."

When Flanagan won, Democratic leadership released a statement that took shots at remarks Tafoya made about the rising price of gas.

"I think right now at least just kind of keeping a stiff upper lip. Maybe you take one less trip to Starbucks and so that gas goes a little further," Tafoya told Tennessee's KWAM radio in March.

Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) and Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), the Senate Minority Leader, called Tafoya "a wealthy Republican activist" out of touch with "struggling Minnesotans."

Should Tafoya win, it would be the first time in 20 years a Republican has held a Senate seat in Minnesota.

title: Kennedy Center votes to restore Trump's name and close for 2 years, challenging a judge's order
description: The battle over the Kennedy Center's future escalated Thursday as President Donald Trump's allies on the board took new steps to commemorate him with physical changes to the iconic performing arts ins...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The battle over the Kennedy Center's future escalated Thursday as President Donald Trump's allies on the board took new steps to commemorate him with physical changes to the iconic performing arts institution that could defy a federal court order.

During an hourslong meeting that was conducted virtually, the board voted to add Trump's name to the building's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump." The plaza in front of the building would be named after Trump and most of the space at the venue would be closed for two years to allow for substantial renovations.

The changes, described by Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who is an ex-officio board member, and her lawyers, amount to a dramatic test of U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper.

He ruled in May that letters affixed to the building that spelled out Trump's name were added illegally and he ordered their removal, a decision that the Republican administration failed to persuade courts to overturn. At the same time, Cooper blocked a two-year closure that was set to take effect July 5, saying an earlier board vote authorizing the shuttering was "ill-informed and seemingly preordained."

"This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court's ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed," Beatty said in a statement. "I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument."

A Kennedy Center representative did not respond to a request for comment.

Much of Thursday's board meeting was expected to focus on the extent of closures required to allow for renovations that the Kennedy Center's management says are needed to improve safety. In response to the judge's criticism of the earlier vote, the institution's leaders said they would provide the board with three options to consider.

They included a complete closure or a partial closure that would allow "some continued public access and limited programming in spaces unaffected" by the work. A third option would "consider a highly limited series of phased closures to address only the Center's most serious infrastructure needs while scheduling and maintaining a full slate of programming."

Ultimately, the board decided to close the building for two years while leaving the potential for some degree of programming to still happen in an outdoor space known as the Reach. The decision to move ahead with the two-year closure, in addition to the moves to memorialize Trump, could revive questions about whether the board seriously considered the full range of options, a point Democrats emphasized after the meeting.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat who is also an ex officio board member, criticized a "sham meeting."

"What happened today was nothing more than a rubber stamp on a decision the President made months ago that the Board already tried to effectuate without doing proper due diligence," he said in a statement.

During Trump's second term, the Kennedy Center has become an unlikely — and highly visible — metaphor for presidential power. While he largely ignored the institution during his first term in Washington, Trump moved quickly to oust its leadership when he returned to office in January 2025 and replaced it with a board of trustees that named him chairman.

His name was quickly added to the building, before coming down in June in response to Cooper's order. The area where it once stood is now covered by a massive tarp.

The Kennedy Center moves are part of Trump's broader push to reshape the physical landscape of the nation's capital in ways that have few modern parallels.

He demolished the East Wing of the White House and is building a controversial ballroom in its place, though an appeals court ruled last week that construction should stop because Congress didn't approve the project. Trump has said he will take the case to the Supreme Court.

His remodel of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has also stumbled after algae returned and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro refuted his claims that a vandal was responsible for the damage.

Meanwhile, Trump is planning extensive renovations of a golf course in East Potomac Park, which could significantly reduce the public's access to running and biking paths. He is also moving forward with a triumphal arch that will sit near Arlington National Cemetery.

Trump has derided the Kennedy Center as "rusted, rotted, and rat and bug infested" and threatened to hand the building over to Congress after Cooper rejected the closure and the addition of the president's name to the building.

The institution's leadership has argued that it's in genuine need of repair and updating.

Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's executive director and chief operating officer, guided a group of journalists through the building in April, highlighting severe water damage that he said corroded steel in some places as thin as tissue paper. Some pieces of equipment, including several 800-ton chillers that help cool the building, are decades old and in need of replacement.

At the time, Floca said he considered doing the repairs individually but insisted it was his recommendation to Trump to close the building and move forward with the renovation all at once.

"When the president asked, 'How do you make these projects the best? How do you make them really excellent and deliver them efficiently?' My recommendation was you close the building and you do everything over a definite period of time, two years," he said.

More recently, the legal battles became the subject of barbs and jokes as comedian Bill Maher accepted the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in late June. At the start of the program, Pamella Roland DeVos, a Kennedy Center trustee appointed by Trump, described the institution as a "national cultural center open not just for some but for every American patron who wants to experience the greatest art and expression the world has to offer."

"The responsibility that comes with it is one our board takes very seriously," she said.

title: Human Rights Watch says the Taliban detained 6 staff of a women’s and children’s rights group
description: Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities have “forcibly disappeared” six staff members of a local organization working on women’s and children’s rights, a U.S.-based advocacy group said, following a separate...
fullText:
ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — Afghanistan's Taliban authorities have "forcibly disappeared" six staff members of a local organization working on women's and children's rights, a U.S.-based advocacy group said, following a separate U.N. report that two Afghan employees of its mission in the country were detained.

The reported detentions come as Afghanistan's Taliban rulers prepare to mark the fifth anniversary of their return to power on Saturday.

The six men — employees of the Women and Children Legal Research Foundation — were detained on July 18 after they were told to come to their office to retrieve confiscated laptops and phones, Human Rights Watch said in a statement released late Wednesday. Their families were given no information about their whereabouts, their condition or possible charges.

Human Rights Watch called on the Taliban to allow family and lawyers to visit the detained and for them to be "immediately released unless they have been charged with a recognizable offense."

The statement came after the U.N. said two Afghan members of its political mission were detained on Sunday in the western city of Herat by the Taliban's General Directorate of Intelligence. The U.N. mission has not been informed of the charges against the two men or been able to visit them, U.N. deputy spokesman Farhan Haq told reporters.

The mission has called on the Taliban "to ensure compliance with the privileges and immunities of the United Nations and its officials," Haq said.

There was no immediate comment on the two incidents from the Taliban, which seized power on Aug. 15, 2021, as U.S. and NATO forces withdrew from the country after two decades of war.

Shortly after taking power, it barred girls from secondary schools and later extended the restrictions to higher education, employment and other sectors, effectively excluding women and girls from public life.

"The Taliban seems to consider any effort to assist women and girls a threat to their abusive rule," said Macarena Sáez, women's rights director at Human Rights Watch. "They should immediately provide information on the six staff members' whereabouts and release them if held unlawfully."

Human Rights Watch said the detention of the six employees came a month after the security forces searched and sealed their office in Kabul and interrogated staff members about their work.

The U.N. mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, said Thursday it had no information on the reported six detentions or whether the two incidents were connected.

The detentions come as a humanitarian crisis in the poverty-stricken Asian nation is worsening and as Taliban forces are engaged in cross-border fighting with Pakistani forces. Clashes escalated sharply in February when Afghan forces launched a raid into Pakistan in retaliation for Pakistani airstrikes inside Afghanistan. Islamabad later declared it was in "open war."

The U.N. mission's mandate from the U.N. Security Council includes promoting and supporting humanitarian assistance to the Afghan people, promoting human rights, equality for women and girls, inclusive governance and economic stability.

title: Nigeria to miss Women's World Cup after South Africa and Ghana win play-offs
description: South Africa and Ghana progress to an inter-confederation qualifier for the 2027 Women's World Cup, but Nigeria will miss the tournament for the first time.
fullText:
Nigeria have failed to qualify for the Fifa Women's World Cup for the first time after they were beaten 2-1 by South Africa in a play-off at the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon).

The continent's top-ranked team went into the tournament in Morocco as favourites to retain their title but were eliminated in the quarter-finals by Cameroon, having already lost to Malawi in the group stage.

With the four semi-finalists guaranteed a spot at next year's World Cup, Justin Madugu's side had one more chance to keep alive their hopes of reaching Brazil, with the winner of their one-off tie in Casablanca entering an inter-confederation qualifier.

But second-half goals from Thembi Kgatlana and Refiloe Jane were enough to give Banyana Banyana victory, despite unexpected late drama when Jane was sent off after picking up a second yellow card for handling the ball inside her own six-yard box.

Christy Ucheibe slotted home the penalty in the 93rd minute to set up a grandstand finish, and there was even time for goalkeeper Kaylin Swart, South Africa's hero, to save brilliantly with her feet to deny Michelle Alozie with almost the last kick of the game.

The 2022 Wafcon champions join Ghana in Fifa's inter-confederation qualifier after the Black Queens came from behind to beat Ivory Coast 2-1 earlier on Thursday.

Nigeria have appeared at all nine Women's World Cups since the first was held in China in 1991.

Missing out is unlikely to go down well in a country where football fans are used to their team dominating, with the Super Falcons having won Wafcon a record 10 times.

But seeing off Desiree Ellis' well-drilled Banyana team was never likely to be easy.

While the first half in Casablanca was a non-event, the second period was anything but, with chances aplenty.

Asisat Oshoala should have done better when she bundled her way through several challenges and poked goalwards from inside the six-yard box, failing to get the requisite power on her strike to trouble Swart.

The six-time African footballer of the year was subbed soon after and there will no doubt be questions about whether the 31-year-old might have appeared at her final Wafcon.

The breakthrough came on the counter in the 56th minute, with striker Ronnel Donnelly playing an exquisite through ball from midway inside her own half to set Hildah Magaia free.

Magaia's cross from the left was met by the onrushing Kgatlana, whose shot had enough power to sneak over the line despite keeper Chiamaka Nnadozie getting a strong hand to it.

Nnadozie did keep out another Kgatlana effort five minutes later, while Swart pulled off a stunning save from Uchenna Kanu's header, diving acrobatically to her left to palm the ball away one-handed.

Jane's goal came courtesy of a deflection off Ucheibe's outstretched foot in the 77th minute and Magaia should also have scored when clean through less than a minute after the restart.

It looked as if Nigeria would be unable to create a way back into the game until Jane's unnecessary handball was spotted by the video assistant referee (VAR).

The captain did not need to stretch out her arm, with Swart well placed to save on the goalline.

With the numerical advantage, Nigeria piled on the pressure and almost found salvation in the 97th minute when Alozie drilled the ball back across goal, only to see Swart's left boot shoot out to stop it flying into the bottom corner.

Swart and South Africa celebrated their victory with glee, but a place at the World Cup is far from certain.

They must first negotiate a six-team league alongside Ghana in November and December, with Asian sides Uzbekistan and Chinese Taipei, Papua New Guinea from Oceania and Ecuador from South America also involved.

The top two sides from that mini-league will advance to a final inter-continental qualifier in February, with three sides from that booking their spot in Brazil.

In the earlier game in Casablanca, Ivory Coast were awarded a penalty after just 44 seconds when Bernadette Kakounan was clipped by Princess Marfo.

After a VAR check, Ines Konan converted to give the Lady Elephants a fourth-minute lead despite Ghana keeper Cynthia Konlan getting a hand to the ball.

The Black Queens thought they had equalised early in the second half when Stella Nyamekye stabbed in, but South African referee Akhona Makalima adjudged that Evelyn Badu had kicked the ball out of the hands of Ivorian keeper Oceane Konan moments before.

Ghana did level in the 59th minute, with Marfo heading in from a corner to make amends for her earlier challenge, and the turnaround was complete when Josephine Bonsu scored from the penalty spot in the 72nd minute after VAR had again intervened.

Grace Asantewaa's fierce strike clearly hit the right arm of Ivory Coast defender Aboa Yapo just inside the area, but it took some deliberation and a trip to the pitch-side monitor before Makalima awarded the foul.

Ghana's victory came a day after the Black Queens squad had issued a statement claiming players and officials were awaiting several payments including Wafcon qualification bonuses, group-stage bonuses and per diem allowances.

Ghana's Ministry of Sports and Recreation challenged aspects of the allegations, with sports minister Kofi Adams insisting that per diem payments had already been settled.

A statement from a Ministry official added that the squad's win bonus from their group stage victory over Cape Verde was being processed, and said that the Black Queens qualifying for Wafcon "does not attract a separate bonus".

title: Warrington crush York to boost top-two hopes
description: Warrington's teenage sensation Ewan Irwin dazzles as Sam Burgess' men beat York Knights at the Halliwell Jones Stadium.
fullText:
Tries: Thewlis, Stone, Irwin, Walker, Lindop Goals: Irwin 5

Tries: McShane, Bennison Goals: Bennison

Warrington Wolves' teenage sensation Ewan Irwin dazzled as Sam Burgess' men beat York Knights at the Halliwell Jones Stadium to turn up the heat in the race for a top-two finish.

Irwin, 18, scored one try and kicked five goals to give notice of the half-back's growing potential as Warrington edged past Wakefield Trinity on points difference into third and they now sit just four points behind leaders Leeds Rhinos.

Josh Thewlis, the returning Sam Stone, Danny Walker and Arron Lindop scored Warrington's other tries in what was the first of three games they will play in 10 hectic days.

York twice took the lead in the first half, with Paul McShane and Jon Bennison scoring for Mark Applegarth's men, before Warrington silenced them.

Heroic Leigh defence denies table-toppers Leeds

Robins stay fifth after beating Dragons

Warrington want home advantage in the play-offs, having won 10 of their past 11 games at the Halliwell Jones, and Tuesday's showdown with fifth-placed Hull KR is mouthwatering.

Cody Hunter created York's opening try after just two minutes when Sam Wood touched back his kick for Bennison to pass inside for McShane to crash over.

In an entertaining clash, Thewlis then pounced on a loose pass to beat three tackles and score a superb converted solo try to give Wire the lead.

Back came York to retake the lead on 19 minutes when Hunter played a super grubber kick through for Bennison to take advantage of hesitation by Warrington to touch down for a converted try.

Warrington showed their class and Stone, who was back after three months out injured, grounded the returning George Williams' kick before Irwin played a dummy to create a gap before charging over to put the home side 16-10 ahead in the 33rd minute.

The teenager then kicked a penalty before half-time to increase Warrington's advantage.

York were tiring and Wire sensed their opportunity, running a penalty after 51 minutes with hooker Walker spinning round to score with Irwin adding the two points.

Irwin was denied a second try when he picked up a loose ball to run 60 yards to score, but the video referee disallowed the score for a knock-on by James Bentley.

York's resistance ended when Hunter was denied a breakaway try when he was ruled offside and 60 seconds later in the 66th minute, Williams kicked for Albert Hopoate to knock the ball inside for Lindop to crash over.

The Betfred player of the match Irwin kicked his second penalty in the final minute to crown his glorious night.

Warrington head coach Sam Burgess told Sky Sports:

On the top two race: "Yeah, we're going as high as we can. We're aiming for the top.

"It's job done. I thought it was a risky night. We had three players coming back from injury and we were a little bit scrappy with the ball. Defensively, we weren't as physical as we could have been, but we're happy to get the two points."

On player of the match, Ewan Irwin: "He's a great kid, he's very balanced. He's got talent, we can all see that. But his greatest attribute is he's a wonderful person. We're all going to see him over the next couple of years."

York head coach Mark Applegarth told BBC Radio York:

"I thought we started brightly. I thought we started full of energy and then Warrington showed their class.

"We spoke at half-time if we tidied up the rucks, we were full of confidence that we could take our chances.

"I think the story of that second half is probably execution and composure. I thought we had enough chances, but the difference is, and why they are where they are in the league and why we are where we are, is they took their chances and we didn't.

"That's the next level we talk about and that we need to get to."

title: GB teenager Nowacki wins dramatic European gold
description: British teenager Filip Nowacki claims a dramatic gold in the men's 200m breaststroke final at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris.
fullText:
British teenager Filip Nowacki claimed a dramatic gold in the men's 200m breaststroke final at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris.

The 18-year-old finished with a late burst in two minutes 7.70 seconds to edge out Dutch swimmer Caspar Corbeau (2:07.78).

Luka Mladenovic of Austria was third (2:08.91), while Briton Gregory Butler finished fifth in 2:09.45.

Nowacki made history for Jersey last month by claiming gold in the 200m breaststroke at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Meanwhile, Lauren Cox and Freya Colbert both won bronze medals for Great Britain.

Cox was third in the women's 50m backstroke final as 19-year-old Italian Sara Curtis won the race in a world record time of 26.56s.

Curtis broke Australian Kaylee McKeown's previous record by 0.23 seconds with a time of 26.63s in the semi- final on Wednesday and improved on that with her victory a day later.

Mary-Ambre Moluh of France was second with 27.06 and Cox was third in 27.15.

Colbert was third, with 1:55.81, in the women's 200m freestyle final as she finished behind winner Barbora Seemanova, who set a championship record of 1:54.38, with Marrit Steenbergen of the Netherlands second in 1:54.65.

Meanwhile, France's Florent Manaudou, who won the 50m freestyle gold at the 2012 Olympics, has said he will retire after his participation at the European Aquatics Championships.

The 35-year-old claimed bronze in the men's 50m freestyle at the 2024 Olympics in Paris and told France TV: "Two years later, I'm announcing the end."

Overall, Manaudou won six Olympic medals across four appearances at the Games, with three silvers and two bronzes in addition to his gold.

title: The level-headed Swede orchestrating magic with Motherwell
description: Alfred Johansson's impressive early work at Motherwell continues with a place in the Conference League play-offs - but don't expect the Swede to get carried away.
fullText:
Motherwell fans are digging out their passports, discovering all sorts of routes to Freiburg and dreaming of the Conference League.

But manager Alfred Johansson's sole focus is on Stenhousemuir in the Scottish League Cup. That was once he had fed his babies to allow his wife to sleep on Thursday night.

The Swede was smiling as his players were serenaded by 8,000-plus supporters at a raucous Fir Park following their wonderful 2-0 win over HJK Helsinki, securing a 3-1 aggregate victory, on a magical night under the lights, but he was - once again - not getting sucked into the conversation of what comes next in European competition.

Their star man - and showman - Ibrahim Said, who former team-mate Andy Halliday said would "be playing for Barcelona if he could score", was, though.

Front and centre of the celebrations following his sublime pair of solo goals, the Nigerian, hailed by Johansson as "outstanding", sent supporters off into the night twisting and shouting to his tune.

While they're, rightly, scrolling through Skyscanner, the wily manager - who remains unbeaten in six matches since succeeding the mighty impressive Jens Berthel Askou - will only be checking out potential road closures on the way to Ochilview on Sunday.

Said's outrageous double sends Motherwell past HJK

All the best Motherwell content in one place

In a way, Johansson had one of the most unenviable jobs upon his appointment. Filling the very large boots left by Askou.

Despite only spending one season in the Scottish Premiership, the Dane attracted so many admirers - far beyond Lanarkshire - through his approach, attitude and style of football.

It's remarkable how seamlessly Johansson has picked up where he left off. Even more so considering key performers Elijah Just, Elliot Watt, Callum Slattery and Calum Ward also moved on.

Few people had a better view of the now-Toulouse boss' brilliance than Halliday - who spent his last playing year under Askou's eye - and he says "a lot of the fundamentals are very similar" under Johansson.

Halliday, who apparently jumped out his seat at Said's second goal against the Finns, added on BBC Sportsound: "I love what Motherwell stand for, how progressive they are, trying to do it a completely different way that's proven, surely to everyone, that it can work.

"Squad development, the youth academy, playing a brilliant brand of football and the fact they lost a fantastic coach and manager last year to go out and recruit similar, I love it."

Invested like many others, the former midfielder does maintain that a signing or two - particularly a goalscoring forward - would be the final piece of the captivating puzzle.

"In wider Scottish football, I hope people sit up and take note of what they're doing," Halliday added.

"I really hope they sign one or two more players at the top end of the pitch, because if they do that, I think they could be every bit as good as last year."

From a media perspective, Johansson is annoyingly level-headed.

In Helsinki, he wouldn’t look forward to this second leg, instead only Falkirk. Here, he only cares about Marvin Bartley's second-tier side. Don’t even bother trying to get an answer on Freiburg.

In the same way he complimented Said's sensational double, the Swede still brought the player back down to earth - as much as possible, anyway - by saying he "didn't manage to show his offensive skills" against Falkirk last weekend.

He is effortlessly grounded. An imperative quality to have while many others get giddy at his side's play and their contribution to the coefficient.

But he's far from a party-pooper, instead feeding off the brilliant and bouncing atmosphere generated round the soulful stands.

"We had 8,100 people at Fir Park tonight which is from what I hear in modern times, if not the best, it's at least up there in terms of attendance," the manager added.

"I'm so pleased, happy and proud to be a part of that.

"When you're in the dugout and the players play on the pitch, there's an energy at Fir Park that transmits down to the pitch.

"It makes us better, it makes us stronger."

They'll be back here in their numbers to do it all again on Thursday, before making the jaunt to Germany, daring to dream.

But up first, Stenny on Sunday. "A final for us," Johansson says.

title: English makes history with European 800m gold
description: Mark English becomes the first man to win a gold medal for Ireland at the European Athletics Championships as he wins the 800m in Birmingham.
fullText:
Mark English has become the first man to win a gold medal for Ireland at the European Athletics Championships after he won the 800m in Birmingham.

English moved into first place inside the final 100 metres as he surged past Croatia's Marino Bloudek to win with a time of one minute 45.26 seconds.

Ben Pattison was sixth, while there was disappointment for his Great Britain team-mate Max Burgin, who was forced to withdraw from the final after he sustained an injury in the warm-up.

But the night belonged to English, who finally won European gold after his bronze medals from 2014 in Zurich and four years ago in Munich.

The 33-year-old was the favourite for gold after he broke Olaf Beyer's 48-year European record in his semi-final at Alexander Stadium.

And while he did not lead the final until he passed the hard-charging Bloudek turning on to the home straight, he delivered in style and fell to his knees as he crossed the line.

The gold for the Donegal runner, who is a qualified doctor, was the first medal of the Championships for Ireland before Rhasidat Adeleke claimed women's 200m silver in the following race.

Ireland's previous gold at a European Championships came when Ciara Mageean won 1500m gold in Rome two years ago.

Hunt surges to 200m glory to win second European gold

English won his first European medal - a bronze - as a 21-year-old in 2014, and was third in Munich in 2022.

"It's just relief. I have been trying for a lifetime to get a title," English told BBC Sport.

"It was relief in 2014 when I got my first medal and relief today as well. It is just amazing.

"I have made a few changes, moved to a new coach [Justin Rinaldi] and he has been amazing. Amazing in terms of advice before races. I have to give big praise to him."

Bloudek of Croatia held on to win silver and Spain's Mohamed Attaoui claimed bronze.

Pattison, the sole British runner after the injury to Burgin, was in a strong position heading into the final 100m but fell short of a medal.

"I'm gutted. It was a great opportunity today to add to my medal collection," Pattison said.

"I gave myself too much work to do, and the legs weren't there. I'm just disappointed."

In the race after English's historic win, Ireland won their second medal of the night as Adeleke took silver in the women's 200m behind home favourite Amy Hunt.

After an injury-plagued year, Adeleke only returned to action at the Irish National Championships to qualify for Birmingham.

The 23-year-old made a strong start and put in a late charge, and while Hunt was clear out in front, Adeleke was able to pip Dina Asher-Smith on the line by just 0.01 seconds, in a time of 22.28 - a new Irish record.

It is a fourth European medal for Adeleke, who claimed a silver in the 400m in Rome two years ago.

She also won gold in the mixed 4x400m relay and a silver in the women's relay at the same Championships.

Later that year, she finished fourth at the Paris Olympics in the 400m but, after an injury-hit two years since, it marks a return to form as she returned to the European podium.

"I had to catch myself at the end because I was thinking I didn't win," Adeleke told BBC Sport.

"Once it sank in, I embraced it. A national record. I cannot believe it. If you knew what my journey looked like and where I was at this year - I barely made it here. I made it here on the last day. I qualified at the nationals.

"Now, I am here and I have won a medal. It has been really hard."

With Commonwealth Games champion Kate O'Connor to come in the heptathlon, against the returning Katarina Johnson-Thompson, there are hopes the Irish medal rush has not finished yet.

title: Beer, wine or liquor? Massive study reveals which was linked to lower death risk
description: Heavy alcohol use raised death risk by 24%, but wine at low levels was linked to lower mortality than beer or spirits in a UK Biobank study.
fullText:
Heavy drinking has been shown to raise mortality risk, but, at lower levels, what's in your glass may also matter, a new study suggests.

In recent research of data from 340,924 participants in the UK Biobank, wine was linked to lower mortality, while beer and spirits were tied to higher death risk.

Data were collected between 2006 and 2022, with more than 13 years of average follow-up. The findings were presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session in New Orleans.

Wine Expert Says One Common Habit Could Be Sabotaging Every Sip

In the study, participants reported their alcohol intake as never/occasional, low, moderate or high.

High consumption was defined as more than 40 grams per day for men (about three standard drinks) and more than 20 grams per day for women (about 1.4 standard drinks).

Participants with high alcohol consumption had a 24% higher risk of all-cause death, 36% higher risk of cancer death and 14% higher risk of cardiovascular death when compared to people who never or occasionally drank, according to the study findings.

With low or moderate alcohol consumption, however, the mortality risk appeared to differ according to the type of beverage.

America Hits Major Marijuana Milestone As Daily Weed Use Surpasses Daily Drinking

Spirits, beer and cider were associated with significantly higher mortality, the researchers found, while the same amount of wine intake was linked to significantly lower mortality. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular death than those who never or occasionally drank.

Conversely, those who drank low amounts of spirits, beer or cider were found to have a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," Dr. Zhangling Chen, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author, said in a press release.

"These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed but also on the type of beverage."

One potential reason for wine's lower mortality association could be that it contains compounds such as polyphenols and antioxidants, which could have beneficial effects on blood vessels, inflammation and cardiovascular health, the researchers noted.

Jessica Steinman, a Los Angeles addiction specialist and chief clinical officer for No Matter What Recovery, said the study's information is "helpful" but cautioned against broadly applying the findings to individuals, particularly those with a history of substance misuse.

Home Cocktail Maker Says Gen Z Isn't Giving Up Alcohol — They're Changing How They Drink

While certain ingredients or substances might help someone with a specific issue, she expressed her concern when it comes to mental health issues and addiction.

"When we hear these stories or get this research, it becomes a 'black and white' larger generalization for the population, and we want to be careful with that," Steinman, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.

"Not everybody should have daily consumption of an alcoholic substance, whether it's wine, beer or certain liquors. … If there's someone who's struggling with substances, then they really shouldn't be having it at all."

Different substances have different levels of alcohol in them, and each person metabolizes alcohol uniquely, the expert noted.

"All those kinds of things are so specific to one person or a small sect of people," she said. "So, we want to make sure anytime there's research given about something, that we're not taking it as a society and saying, 'Let's do this,' and not keeping it as black and white.

Click Here For More Health Stories

"Overall, more is not better, but also the higher potency of alcohol and higher percentages of alcohol is going to affect people negatively as well."

Steinman recommended consulting with a medical professional for individual guidance.

The researchers acknowledged some limitations of the study. Because it was observational in design, the study could not prove that drinking wine led to lower mortality or that other alcoholic beverages directly caused higher mortality.

Also, the participants reported their baseline alcohol intake at the start of the study, which means any changes in drinking patterns during the follow-up period were not recorded.

Test Yourself With Our Latest Lifestyle Quiz

There was also the chance that wine drinkers may have different dietary or other lifestyle habits that could affect their health outcomes, the researchers noted.

The UK Biobank participants also tend to be healthier than the overall population, which could limit the ability for the finding to be generalized to wider populations.

The authors called for high-quality randomized studies to confirm the differences in how drinking habits reflect mortality risk.

title: WW2 veterans fly in Spitfires for first time
description: Ivan Staines, Alfred Cooley and Paul Terry take off in the iconic aircraft from Biggin Hill Airport.
fullText:
Three World War Two veterans have fulfilled a long-held ambition by flying in Spitfires for the first time.

The former servicemen took to the skies above Kent from the heritage hangar at London's Biggin Hill Airport on Thursday watched by family members and fellow veterans.

Ivan Staines, 99, Alfred Cooley, 100, and Paul Terry, 101, had all served during the war, but none of the three had flown in a Spitfire before.

The flights were organised by the Taxi Charity for Military Veterans, which is run by black cab drivers, and paid for with a fund set up to make World War Two veterans' wishes come true.

Cooley told how he was "absolutely blown away".

He said: "The experience was something I will remember for the rest of my life. I never thought that one day I would be flying in my favourite plane - the spitfire.

"I used to see them flying over my head when I was 13 years old and war had just started."

Staines played with his five-year-old great-grandson Alfie Rose in the hangar before the flight.

The veteran had served in the Home Guard from 1942 to 1944, when he was called up to fight in Europe, aged 18.

He was transferred to the South Staffordshire Regiment and later deployed to Palestine.

After the flight, Staines said it was "an amazing experience that I never expected to get".

"I am absolutely over the moon," he added.

Cooley signed up to the Highland Light Infantry's 5th Battalion the day before D-Day, and after eight weeks' training, he landed in a liberated France at the age of 18, and travelled towards the German border.

His daughter Ann Crossley said: "Today is the day my wonderful dad gets to fulfil his wish to fly in a Spitfire."

She said the family was "so grateful" to the charity for the places he had seen and camaraderie he had experienced, adding: "He has so many new friends in this fantastic 'family' and is loving every minute of it."

Joining them was Paul Terry, from the King's Royal Rifle Corps, one of three brothers who survived the war.

Terry landed in Normandy the day after D-Day and later travelled through France, Belgium and Holland.

He fought in operation Market Garden to secure Nijmegen Bridge, before he moved on to Arnhem.

Terry said the flight was "remarkably smooth, though to be honest, not quite as fast as I thought". He said: "I reckon my BMW could give it a run for its money."

​The veteran said: "Jokes aside, it was an incredible experience.

"From watching the dogfights rage over London as a teenager, to spending the war as a rifleman with my feet planted firmly on terra firma, finally getting up into the sky in a Spitfire brought everything full circle."

Keely Allen, the charity's trustee and fundraising officer, said: "Seeing Paul, Alf and Ivan take to the skies in three Spitfires has been an incredibly moving and proud moment for everyone involved.

"These iconic aircraft played such an important part in the story of their generation, so to see them flying in one is something very special."

"We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment. What they do in ⁠those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls — it's incredible," Hegseth told reporters during a visit to Panama.

Typically naval deployments are ⁠for between six and nine months, but during times of conflict, that can be extended.

Extended deployments can pose enormous strain on crews' mental health, particularly in wartime, and have always been a challenge ​for the ​U.S. Navy. Sailors must maintain a heightened state ​of alert and readiness, especially with ‌the threat of drone and missile attack from Iran.

A U.S. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the George Washington aircraft carrier is heading to the region with the intention of replacing the Lincoln carrier. That move was pre-planned, the official said.

Democratic lawmakers are unhappy about the extended deployment of the Lincoln carrier and the conditions on the ship.

title: Kerr's Europeans absence ruining the sport - Ingebrigtsen
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen says he is "very" disappointed by British rival Josh Kerr's decision to miss the European Championships in Birmingham.
fullText:
Jakob Ingebrigtsen says he is "very" disappointed Britain's Josh Kerr is not competing at the European Championships, claiming that athletes who choose to miss major competitions are "ruining" the sport.

Ingebrigtsen secured a stunning 5,000m gold on his long-awaited return from injury on Monday, becoming the joint-most successful athlete in European Championships history.

After 11 months out of competition, during which he underwent surgery on his Achilles, the 25-year-old wasted no time in reigniting his fierce rivalry with Kerr.

Last month, Kerr smashed the mile world record, which had stood for 27 years, before winning Commonwealth gold over the distance on home soil in Glasgow.

The Scot made clear the Europeans were never part of his plans this season, but Ingebrigtsen believes Kerr should have been able to include it in his schedule.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Ingebrigtsen was complimentary of Kerr's record-breaking performance in London but said he "could never" prioritise a time over a title.

"Of course I am going to go for times, but I don't think you have to do one or the other," Ingebrigtsen said.

Asked if he was disappointed Kerr is not racing in Birmingham, he added: "Very - and I think a lot of people should be, because that is what championships are all about.

"It's not for us as athletes to choose almost where to participate. We have these championships for a reason, and that is for the best athletes to compete - that is the whole point.

"So I definitely think it is ruining the sport if we are not participating. We all have different plans, but I could never see myself in that position."

The rivalry between Kerr and Ingebrigtsen has developed into one of the sport's most compelling storylines over recent years.

Having taken Olympic 1500m bronze behind gold medal-winner Ingebrigtsen five years ago, Kerr stunned his rival at the World Championships in Budapest in 2023 to set up one of the most eagerly-anticipated showdowns of the Paris 2024 Olympics.

As their war of words continued in the lead-up to that event, Ingebrigtsen claimed he could beat Kerr blindfolded when fully fit, while Kerr said the Norwegian had "flaws on the track and in the manners realm" and is surrounded by "yes men".

In giving everything to defeat the other, they were beaten to gold by American Cole Hocker.

Things have cooled since then as Ingebrigtsen struggled with injury, but he has announced his return to the top by winning a record seventh European Championship gold - his 20th major international track title since 2018.

Ingebrigtsen said Kerr's record-breaking run was an "extremely good race" and "a very strong performance".

But, in weighing up whether he feels that is as important as winning titles, he said: "I think both are as big, but it is not like we only have one race in our legs.

"Everything comes down to what you want to do. People go to work every day. It is not like because you are a professional runner you can't work every day."

title: 'Dad rang and I was like: What's happening?' - England U20s boss on Uefa threat
description: England head coach Lydia Bedford says she has been told to "just continue as usual" before next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup, despite the threat of a Uefa boycott over an ongoing row with Fifa.
fullText:
England's head coach Lydia Bedford says she has been told by the Football Association to "just continue as usual" before next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup, despite Uefa threatening to boycott the tournament.

Bedford said she had not "thought too much about the bigger picture" as she prepares to name her Young Lionesses squad next week.

Football has been engulfed in a major dispute since it emerged that Fifa president Gianni Infantino was planning to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.

Uefa and its 55 members threatened to boycott Fifa competitions, and that still stands despite the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal having been abandoned earlier this month with the Under-20 Women's World Cup the first tournament that could be impacted.

Speaking to BBC Sport in Portugal after England had won a warm-up game against Portugal, Bedford spoke for the first time about the potential boycott.

"I was actually at the theatre in London when my dad rang me out of the blue and I was like 'what's happening?' From my perspective the message from leadership all along has been 'just continue as usual' so we have," she said.

"It's not something we've really even spoken to the players about because ultimately every opportunity we have to get on the grass and prepare this team we want to be in the best position possible.

"So all focus has been on that."

Women's football shouldn't be penalised by Uefa boycott - Nandy

Six European teams are set to take part in the tournament, which runs from 5-27 September, and BBC Sport understands none of them have told hosts Poland that they are withdrawing.

Poland's attacking midfielder Weronika Arasniewicz also spoke to BBC Sport and outlined her opposition to a proposed boycott.

"Don't do it. Let the football be there. Let's enjoy football," Arasniewicz said.

"I would be disappointed for sure [if the tournament was cancelled] because events like this, it's always special and you don't know how many World Cups you have ahead of you."

While some players oppose the boycott, England international Lucy Bronze recently said that boycotting Fifa competitions would be the right thing "for the good of the game", despite the impact it could have on women's football.

Asked about those comments, Bedford said: "From my perspective my only focus is preparing this team to be ready and if we have the opportunity to go to Poland we will be there and punching when we arrive.

"So I haven't thought too much about the bigger picture but my message has been continue as usual and that is what we are going to continue to do."

Bedford was appointed as England women's Under-23s coach in March, and as part of that role is leading the Young Lionesses for the tournament in Poland.

On Thursday, her side beat Portugal U20s 2-0 in a friendly in Lisbon.

"I'm really proud of the players," she said. "From start to finish today we showed our quality and our depth in this squad.

"I have an incredibly difficult decision to make next week to pick the team that finally goes."

Asher-Smith was beaten to silver by just 0.01 seconds by Ireland's Rhasidat Adeleke, who set a new national record.

"It unfolded exactly how I thought it would," two-time European 200m silver medallist Nethaneel Mitchell-Blake said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I knew Dina would run a blistering bend and then say 'Amy, come and catch me'. And that's what Amy has done."

After struggling in the 200m earlier this summer, Hunt said she was ready for a "renewal of our vows" in the event.

And the Briton kept her promise with a composed performance that ended with her powering through the final 40m to beat her competitors and clinch gold.

"Amy was phenomenal. She came off that bend like a train," three-time world heptathlon champion Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill said on BBC TV.

"It was so exciting to see Dina and Amy side by side. Amy said she was going to do it - and she did."

Hunt held her arms aloft and pointed to the sky as she emulated Asher-Smith's 100m-200m European double in 2018.

"Amy has it all. The speed, the endurance, the confidence, and now the double," said former men's 1500m world champion Steve Cram.

"This is Amy's stage at the moment."

After getting off to a rapid start, Asher-Smith was unable to hold off Hunt and Adeleke in the final push, but in finishing third she claimed a ninth European medal - a tally only bettered by the 10 of Polish ex-sprinter Irena Szewinska.

"Dina was not handing it to Amy. She was going to make her work hard," former British 400m runner Allison Curbishley said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Asher-Smith held on as hard as she could. Then she started to over-stride, and the hips dropped."

After finishing fifth in Monday's 100m final, Asher-Smith returned for the 200m to continue her bid to win a historic seventh gold and become the joint-most successful athlete in the history of the championships.

But there was further disappointment for the 30-year-old, who won European 200m gold in 2016 and 2018.

"I'm disappointed to have a bronze, but I think 10 years after my first one it is such an achievement to be in a place to come back year after year," Asher-Smith told BBC TV.

"It doesn't matter what's going on in my life, just come and continue to be one of the fastest women in the world. Happy to have done that today."

Before the race, there were hopes of a British one-two-three on the podium, with Asher-Smith, Hunt and Eduan holding the three fastest times in Europe this year.

However, Eduan - who beat Hunt to win her first British title in June - finished sixth.

But Hunt's second sprint gold continues Britain's dominance in the sprint events in Birmingham after Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu secured a one-two finish in the men's 100m, while Matthew Hudson-Smith stormed to 400m victory on Wednesday.
